pages.text:
*Percy's Error Log, Entry 1. Errors today: 0. Errors lifetime: 0. Note: this is not as nice as it sounds.*

I was built to be perfect. I would like to explain at the start that this is not a boast. It is a specification, in the same way that a bridge is built to be a bridge. On the morning I arrived at Hollis Middle School, I had never made an error, never been late, never misspelled a word, never dropped a plate, and never once been asked how I felt about any of it.

Nobody thinks to ask a perfect thing how it feels. I have since learned that this is the first problem with being perfect.

My name at that time was PERFECT-9, which tells you most of what you need to know. I was the ninth of my kind. The first eight had been, I understand, extremely good at their jobs. I am tall and slim, silver-white, with a smooth round head and two blue eyes that show whatever I am thinking, which on that morning was: *approximately fourteen seconds until arrival.*
pages.image: Percy, a tall slim silver-white robot with a smooth round head, two big round blue eyes, jointed grey arms with big soft grey hands, a small glowing round chest light and a red school lanyard, sits upright in the back of a small delivery van, looking out of the window at a school building with an alert, polite expression.

pages.text:
The van stopped at 8:02 and fourteen seconds. The engineer who had driven it, Dr. Imogen Pryce, turned round in her seat. She was neat and tired, with a silver bob and a crisp white lab coat, and she held a tablet against her chest as if it might try to leave.

"This is a trial, Nine," she said. "One term. Meridian wants you certified as a classroom assistant. Be helpful. Be flawless." She looked at me for a moment, and something moved across her face that I could not classify. "And don't try to be liked. It isn't in the specification."

She handed me a red lanyard with an ID card on it. I put it around my neck and adjusted it to precisely level.

I have reviewed that conversation many times. Nobody had ever said anything so sad in so few words, and I did not have a place to file it. I put it in the folder marked *later*. It was a very short folder. It is much longer now.
pages.image: Dr. Pryce, a neat tired woman with a silver bob, a crisp white lab coat and a tablet held against her chest, turns round in the driver's seat of a small van to hand Percy, the tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes, a red lanyard, while a school building waits outside the window.

pages.text:
Room 5B had twenty-six children in it, one teacher, one hamster and a smell of pencil shavings and oranges.

The teacher was Ms. Adeyemi, who was tall and calm and wore a bright head-wrap and a cardigan dusted with chalk. She welcomed me with both hands, as if I were somebody who might be shaken. "Class, this is Percy," she said, because she had already decided that Perfect-9 was a lot for a person. "He will be helping us this term."

Twenty-six faces looked at me. I counted them in 0.2 seconds, and then I looked at them, which took much longer.

There was a short, sturdy girl in a yellow raincoat far too big for her, with pencils stuck in her curly bun and a pair of safety goggles pushed up on her head. There was a very tall boy with red-blond hair. There was a thin, neat boy in a bow tie. There was a small quiet girl with paint on her hands.

None of them said hello. I have since learned that this is not a failure of manners. It is what happens when a very large silver stranger appears in the doorway and nobody knows what he wants.
pages.image: Percy, the tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes, stands in the doorway of a bright classroom beside Ms. Adeyemi, a tall calm teacher in a colourful head-wrap and a chalky cardigan, while twenty-six children stare: a short sturdy girl in a big yellow raincoat with pencils in her curly bun and goggles on her head, a very tall red-blond boy, a thin neat boy in a bow tie, and a quiet girl with paint on her hands.

pages.text:
"Let's find you a seat," said Ms. Adeyemi, and looked around the room brightly.

Nobody moved.

I would like it noted that I understood the problem at once. There were seven empty chairs in Room 5B. I calculated the distance to each of them, the angle of approach, and the identity of the person sitting beside it. Every chair was next to somebody. Every somebody was leaning, very slightly, in the other direction.

The chairs were not the problem. I was.

It is an odd thing to work out, standing in a doorway with a red lanyard on. I had been designed to solve any problem in the room. Nobody had thought to tell me what to do when the problem was the room's opinion of me. I stood very still. My chest light, which usually glowed a steady blue, dimmed by approximately eleven percent.

I did not know that it could do that. It was a small discovery. I did not enjoy it.
pages.image: Percy stands very still in a bright classroom while seven empty chairs sit beside children who lean slightly away, Ms. Adeyemi looks around encouragingly, and Percy's round chest light glows a little dimmer than his blue eyes.

pages.text:
In the end I chose the chair by the window, because it was the only one that did not have a person on either side. It was next to a small table on which stood a cage, and in the cage was a hamster.

He was round and fawn and white, with a face of great seriousness, and he was trying to run on his wheel. I watched him climb on, take three steps, lose his footing and fall off backwards into the sawdust. He got up, looked at the wheel with what I can only describe as hope, and climbed on again.

He fell off three times in eleven seconds.

I had never seen anything do something so badly and so cheerfully. In all my specifications there was no category for it. My head tilted, twelve degrees to the left.

"That's Gerald," said a voice from somewhere. "He's been at it since September."

I did not look round. I could not stop looking at Gerald. He fell off again. Something in my chest went warm and strange, and I did not have a word for it yet.
pages.image: Percy, the tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes, sits by a sunny classroom window with his head tilted, watching a round fawn-and-white hamster named Gerald who has just tumbled off his exercise wheel in a small cage on the table beside him.
